lead: A single processor runs one instruction at a time, and its clock cannot keep rising because of heat and power limits. Parallel processing answers this by using many execution units together: several cores on one chip, many lanes inside one core, or hundreds of machines in a cluster. The same idea appears at levels from adding 64 bits in one clock to splitting a training job across 1000 servers. This chapter explains why parallelism is needed, which levels exist, and which design problems every parallel program must solve.

sections.h3: Why one processor is no longer enough

blocks.text: For thirty years each new chip ran faster than the last. That stopped. Clock frequency is now limited by heat. The dynamic power a chip burns rises with the square of the supply voltage and in proportion to the clock, so pushing the clock up makes the chip overheat or drains a phone battery in hours. Engineers call this the power wall.

blocks.where: P is the dynamic power in watts, C is the switched capacitance in farads, V is the supply voltage in volts, and f is the clock frequency in hertz. Halving V cuts P to one quarter (divides it by 4) at the same f.

blocks.text: A second wall is memory. Processor cycles became shorter much faster than DRAM access time did, so one core can wait hundreds of cycles for a single load. Many cores waiting together hide that gap; one very fast core cannot.
A third wall is instruction-level. A superscalar core already issues a few instructions per cycle, and true dependencies between instructions stop it going much wider.

Meanwhile the work grew. A UPI switch clears thousands of transactions every second, and a team training a language model wants billions of arithmetic operations per second. One core delivers neither. The answer is to build machines that do many things at once: several cores on a die, wide vector units, and clusters of machines.
Parallelism is not one thing. It appears at five levels, from a trick inside the adder to a data centre.

items: Bit level: a 64-bit adder works on 64 bit pairs in one operation instead of an 8-bit adder taking eight steps. Carry look-ahead adders are the classic example, since they compute all carries in parallel rather than letting one carry ripple through.

Instruction level: a pipeline overlaps stages of different instructions, so while instruction 1 writes its result, a later instruction (three stages behind in a classic 5-stage pipeline) is decoding, and several instructions are in flight at once. A superscalar core issues two to six instructions in the same cycle.
Data level: one instruction acts on many data items. A vector unit adds eight floating-point numbers per instruction; a GPU runs thousands of lanes on the same instruction over different elements.
Task level: different threads do different jobs on different cores, for example one thread renders video while another plays audio. Threads share data, so synchronisation enters.
Job level: independent programs run on separate machines, such as 500 batch jobs on a cluster.

blocks.text: The levels differ in granularity: the amount of useful work done between two communication or synchronisation events. Bit-level work has no communication at all. A thread hand-off costs tens of nanoseconds, a cluster message microseconds. Fine-grained parallelism needs cheap communication; coarse-grained parallelism tolerates expensive communication. The SIMD and MIMD labels for these machines are in Flynn's models.

sections.h3: Parallel versus distributed, design issues, and the ecosystem

blocks.text: Parallel computing and distributed computing overlap but are not the same. Parallel computing usually means tightly coupled hardware: cores that share one memory, a fast interconnect, one operating system, communication in nanoseconds, and any core able to read what another wrote. Distributed computing means independent computers on a network, each with its own memory and clock, able to fail alone, where messages can be delayed or lost. A 32-core server is parallel; a cloud region or a set of bank ATMs is distributed. See Unit 4, Distributed System Models and Logical Time, for the distributed side.
Every parallel system faces the same five design issues.

items: Partitioning: cut the work into pieces that can run at the same time (Chapter 1.7).
Communication: move data between pieces and count its cost (Chapter 1.5).
Synchronisation: make pieces wait at the right points (Unit 3).
Scalability: keep efficiency as processors are added (Chapter 1.6).
Fault tolerance: keep going when one piece or one machine fails (Unit 5).

blocks.text: Hardware follows the same trade-offs. A multicore CPU gives 8 to 64 powerful cores that share cache. A GPU gives thousands of small lanes with high memory bandwidth. A cluster joins commodity servers on Ethernet or InfiniBand. Cloud instances are rented by the hour. Doubling cores rarely doubles speed, because coordination and idle time grow, and a data centre pays for power and cooling on every core.

examples.question: A program takes 100 s on one processor. Of that run time, 20% is serial work that cannot be parallelised and 80% is parallel work that scales perfectly. (a) Find the maximum speedup with any number of processors. (b) Find the speedup and efficiency with 16 processors. (c) Say in one line why the answer to (b) is not 16.
steps: Let f be the serial fraction and p the number of processors. Here f = 0.20 and the parallel fraction is 1 − f = 0.80.
(a) With p processors the time is T(p) = T(1) × (f + (1 − f)/p). As p grows, the term (1 − f)/p falls to 0, so T(p) → T(1) × f and the speedup is capped at 1/f.
S(max) = 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5. Even with infinite processors the program cannot run more than 5 times faster than one processor.
S(16) = T(1) ÷ T(16) = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, so the run time falls from 100 s to 25 s.
Efficiency = S(16) ÷ p = 4 ÷ 16 = 0.25, that is 25% of the 16 processors' capacity is used.
(c) The remaining 20 s of serial work still runs on one processor, so the time can never drop below 20 s.
examples.answer: (a) Maximum speedup is 5. (b) With 16 processors the speedup is 4 and the efficiency is 0.25 (25%).
examples.check:
serial = 0.20
parallel = 1.0 - serial
max_speedup = 1.0 / serial
p = 16
speedup = 1.0 / (serial + parallel / p)
efficiency = speedup / p
print(max_speedup)
print(speedup)
print(efficiency)

traps: Swapping the fractions: 20% serial means f = 0.20, not 0.80. Always divide 1 by the serial fraction for the unlimited-processor bound.
Assuming speedup equals the number of processors. Amdahl's bound caps it at 1/f, and real machines fall below even that because of overhead.
Calling a multithreaded program on one server 'distributed'. Distributed means separate memories, separate clocks and partial failure; a shared-memory server is parallel.
Confusing granularity with level. Granularity is the work done per communication event; the five levels are where the parallelism sits.

quiz.q: Name the five levels of parallelism, smallest first.
quiz.a: Bit level, instruction level, data level, task (thread) level, job level.

quiz.q: Why did clock frequency stop rising after the mid-2000s?
quiz.a: Dynamic power grows as C × V² × f, so a faster clock makes the chip too hot to cool or drains the battery. Designers added cores instead of raising the clock, which is the power wall.

quiz.q: A program is 10% serial. Find the maximum speedup and the speedup with 8 processors.
A GPU has thousands of lanes and a CPU has 16 cores. Give two reasons the GPU is not always faster for a given program.
quiz.a: The GPU lanes are narrow and need data-parallel work with the same instruction on many elements; a program with branches and dependencies leaves lanes idle. Data must also be moved over the PCIe bus to and from GPU memory, and that transfer cost may exceed the gain.

quiz.q: Define granularity and say why it matters for choosing a machine.
quiz.a: Granularity is the amount of useful work done between two communication or synchronisation events. Fine-grained work needs cheap, fast communication such as shared memory; coarse-grained work tolerates slow, expensive communication such as a cluster network.

quiz.q: Classify each as bit, instruction, data, task or job level: (i) carry look-ahead adder, (ii) OpenMP thread pool on 8 cores, (iii) 500 batch jobs on a cluster, (iv) a vector unit adding 8 floats per instruction.
Why does the serial part of a program limit speedup even when processors are unlimited?
quiz.a: The serial part must run on one processor, so it sets a floor on the total time. If f is the serial fraction of the one-processor time, total time cannot fall below f × T(1), giving a maximum speedup of 1 ÷ f no matter how many processors are added.

beyond: Not for the exam. Chip designers now talk about dark silicon: parts of a chip are switched off at any moment because the whole die cannot run at full clock inside a power budget. Chiplets and 3D stacking are current answers, packing more cores without one huge die. GPUs are also used through libraries rather than hand-written CUDA for most work. Energy per operation, not raw speed, is the number that decides modern data-centre design. Search for 'dark silicon', 'chiplet architecture' and 'roofline model' to go further.
